newsitem.title: NORWAY: Deepwater oil has bright future, but bears risks.
newsitem.headline: Deepwater oil has bright future, but bears risks.

text.p: With much of the world's unexplored acreage lying deep under the sea, demand for deepwater drilling is set to rise rapidly, said Jon Cole, senior vice president of U.S. firm Sonat Offshore Drilling Inc.
But the oil industry must recognise the particular risks involved in operating in water depths of 1,000 metres or more, he warned on Friday.

"With the increase in demand for deep water drilling, offshore rigs are being pushed into deeper water than their original design anticipated," Cole told delegates at the 1996 Offshore Northern Seas conference in Stavanger.
"The drilling industry needs to ensure that increased water depth does not cause a reduction in the environmental criteria and a relaxation of the safety margin of the original design."
Cole said that the deeper the water, the bigger both economic and environmental risks become.
"With a deep water blowout...the potential for pollution, loss of the well, loss of time and higher costs all take on an added importance."
Nevertheless, oil company officials agree that the growth in demand for deep water drilling has just begun.
According to the Texaco Inc -led Deepstar consortium of companies, 95 percent of the world's unexplored acreage lies in water depths of over 900 metres.
At present, deepwater expertise is dominated by just a handful of oil companies -- six operators account for 86 percent of all deep water wells, Cole said.
Also, though deep water operations are scattered throughout the world, almost 75 percent of all activity is concentrated in two regions -- offshore Brazil and the U.S. Gulf of Mexico.
Growth potential is seen both in these established markets and elsewhere.

"In order to increase Petrobras's domestic oil production, it must develop its deepwater fields...around 70 percent of (Brazil's) oil production will come from deepwaters (over 400 metres) in 2005," Antonio Carlos de Agostini, managing director of exploration and production at Brazil's Petrobras told conference delegates.

And deepwater fields over 450 metres will account for 25 to 35 percent of production from the Gulf of Mexico by the turn of the century, compared to four percent in 1995, said Don Henery, manager offshore engineering and pipelines at Shell International.
Shell has two 1,000 metre deepwater projects in the Gulf of Mexico -- Mars and Auger -- and is preparing to plumb even greater depths.
"This can be extended to at least 1,650 metres with the Mensa project...Shell have explored previously in 2,200 metre water depths and are now initiating drilling in 2,400 metres," he said.
Deepwater drilling demand will also be fuelled by emerging demand off Norway and the U.K.

The next areas to look out for are offshore West Africa, the Atlantic margin of the North Sea, and several countries in Southeast Asia which have already attracted exploratory interest, Sonat's Cole said.
